title: Consensus & Leader Election
subtitle: Reach one ordered decision despite delayed messages, crashes, and leadership changes
objectives: Explain why agreement is hard when messages can be lost, delayed, or duplicated
Describe how majority quorums make split-brain impossible rather than unlikely
Walk through leader election, terms, and why a fencing token is required
Decide when you need consensus — and why the answer is usually 'use the thing that already has it'

exercises.title: A timeout suspects failure but cannot prove that a remote node stopped
exercises.body: In an asynchronous network, a missing reply can mean the peer crashed, the request was lost, the response was lost, or either message is delayed. A timeout converts that uncertainty into a local suspicion so the protocol can retry or start an election; it does not establish the peer's state.
exercises.note: Consensus protocols preserve safety despite false suspicions. Progress can pause during prolonged delay because agreement cannot depend on distinguishing delay from failure.

exercises.prompt: A leader acknowledges a write before any follower stores it. Require a majority to store the log entry before acknowledging.
exercises.beforeStatus: LEADER FAILURE · acknowledged write is lost · 1 of 3 copies stored it
exercises.afterStatus: LEADER FAILURE · committed write survives · 2 of 3 copies stored it
exercises.result: The acknowledged write survived leader loss
exercises.why: In a three-node consensus group, storing an entry on a majority means at least two nodes have it before acknowledgment. Election rules must also prevent a candidate missing committed entries from becoming leader; majority storage alone is not the entire protocol.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: A leader acknowledges a write before any follower stores it. Require a majority to store the log entry before acknowledging. Place Leader, Follower A, Follower B. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Client → Leader; Leader → Follower A. That topology is the evidence for the answer: In a three-node consensus group, storing an entry on a majority means at least two nodes have it before acknowledgment. Election rules must also prevent a candidate missing committed entries from becoming leader; majority storage alone is not the entire protocol.

exercises.prompt: Five servers must agree on one value: who is the leader. Why can't they just vote and be done?
choices: Messages can be lost, delayed, or arrive out of order — so a node that hears nothing can't tell whether a vote was never sent, or sent and lost, or is still in flight
exercises.why: A node cannot distinguish a failed peer from a slow peer or a lost message by observing silence. Consensus protocols must preserve one decision despite those ambiguous failures and differing views of which nodes are reachable.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'just add a timeout' not solve it?
choices: A timeout converts 'I don't know' into a guess: too short and you declare a healthy node dead, too long and you stay stuck — the uncertainty doesn't go away, you just pick which way to be wrong
exercises.why: A timeout marks a peer as suspected after no response arrives within a chosen interval. Network delay, packet loss, pauses, and actual peer failure can all produce that observation. Short intervals reduce failure-detection time and increase false suspicions during transient delays; long intervals reduce false suspicions and extend failover time.

exercises.prompt: ______ is the problem of getting multiple machines to agree on a single value despite failures.
exercises.why: Consensus makes nonfailed participants choose one value despite node or network failures. Agreement prevents different machines from committing incompatible leaders, log entries, or configuration state.

exercises.prompt: What goes wrong if two nodes both believe they're the leader?
choices: Nothing — more leaders means more capacity
Both accept writes, producing two divergent histories with no principled way to merge them — split brain
exercises.why: Two leaders can accept conflicting operations and produce divergent histories, a failure called split brain. Consensus restricts leadership and commits to quorum-backed terms so only one authoritative history can advance.

exercises.prompt: What must a consensus algorithm guarantee? Select all.
choices: Agreement — no two nodes decide different values
Validity — the decided value was actually proposed by someone
Termination — it eventually decides, provided enough nodes are up and can communicate
That it always decides quickly, no matter what
exercises.why: Consensus requires agreement, validity of the chosen value, and termination under stated liveness assumptions. The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson result shows that deterministic consensus cannot guarantee termination in a fully asynchronous system with even one crash failure, so practical protocols rely on timing assumptions and may stall.

exercises.prompt: So why is 'agreement' the property worth paying for?
choices: Because conflicting committed decisions can violate an invariant, such as granting one lock to two owners, while a delayed decision preserves safety
exercises.why: Consensus prioritizes safety: nodes may delay a decision when they cannot establish quorum, but they must not commit incompatible values. Some divergent application data can be reconciled later; two simultaneously valid lock owners or incompatible committed log histories can already have triggered irreversible external actions.

exercises.title: Majority quorums intersect in at least one voting member
exercises.body: For `N` configured voters, a majority contains more than `N/2` members. Any two majorities overlap, so disjoint sides of a partition cannot each form a majority under one configuration. In a crash-fault protocol, at most one side can continue quorum-gated work.
exercises.note: The threshold is computed from configured membership, not reachable nodes. Removing failed voters requires a safely committed membership change.

exercises.prompt: 5 nodes. A rule says a decision needs 3 votes. A partition splits them 3 and 2. Why can't both sides decide?
choices: Only one side can hold 3 of 5 — two disjoint groups cannot both contain a majority, so at most one side can ever proceed
The rule is enforced by a coordinator
exercises.why: Any two majorities of the same five-node membership overlap. The three-node side can obtain a majority, while the two-node side cannot, preventing both partition sides from independently electing leaders.

exercises.prompt: Why do consensus clusters use odd numbers of nodes — 3, 5, 7?
choices: 4 nodes need 3 for a majority, exactly like 3 nodes do — so the 4th node adds cost and tolerates no additional failure
Even numbers can't form a majority
exercises.why: Three nodes require two votes and four nodes require three, so both configurations continue after only one unavailable node. Five nodes require three votes and therefore add tolerance for a second unavailable node.

exercises.prompt: A consensus cluster has 7 nodes. How many can fail while the cluster still makes progress?
exercises.why: A seven-node cluster requires four votes for a majority, so it remains live with any four reachable nodes and tolerates three unavailable nodes. In general, `2f+1` voting nodes tolerate `f` unavailable nodes.

exercises.prompt: A write is committed once a majority stored it, and a leader needs a majority to be elected. Is quorum overlap ALONE enough to guarantee the new leader has every committed write?
choices: Yes — the two majorities must overlap, so it's proven
No — overlap only proves some VOTER has the write; you also need the rule that a voter refuses to vote for a candidate whose log is behind its own
Yes, because writes are broadcast to every node
No — committed writes are always lost during a failover
exercises.why: Quorum overlap ensures the election voters include a node with every committed entry, but it does not ensure the candidate has those entries. Raft voters grant a vote only when the candidate's log is at least as up to date as their own, so a candidate missing committed history cannot win.

exercises.prompt: Your 5-node cluster is split into 2 and 2 and 1 by a network fault. What happens?
choices: Nobody has a majority, so the cluster makes no progress at all — it stays consistent by being entirely unavailable
exercises.why: A five-node cluster requires three votes, and no partition group has three. Without a quorum, no leader can be elected and no entry can be committed, preserving one history by making writes unavailable.

exercises.prompt: Is a majority quorum protecting you from nodes that lie or send corrupted messages?
choices: No — algorithms like Raft assume nodes may crash or be unreachable, but not that they actively lie; surviving liars is Byzantine fault tolerance, which is far more expensive
Yes, if you use enough nodes
exercises.why: Raft and Paxos assume crash faults: a node follows the protocol until it stops or becomes unreachable. Byzantine faults allow arbitrary or malicious behavior and require Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols with additional replicas and communication rounds.

exercises.title: A consensus leader assigns one order to proposed operations
exercises.body: Clients send writes to the current leader. The leader appends each operation to its log, assigns its position, replicates the entry to followers, and commits it after the protocol's quorum rule is satisfied. Followers apply committed entries in that order.
exercises.note: In a single-leader design, leader CPU, network, or storage often bounds write throughput. Additional followers primarily add fault tolerance and read capacity.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: A consensus leader assigns one order to proposed operations
exercises.why: Clients send writes to the current leader. The leader appends each operation to its log, assigns its position, replicates the entry to followers, and commits it after the protocol's quorum rule is satisfied. Followers apply committed entries in that order. In a single-leader design, leader CPU, network, or storage often bounds write throughput. Additional followers primarily add fault tolerance and read capacity.

exercises.prompt: Why elect a single leader at all, if consensus can decide any value?
choices: Because one leader proposes a single log order, so followers validate and replicate that order instead of negotiating competing orders for each entry
exercises.why: Consensus elects one leader and establishes its term. The leader assigns log order, then replicates each entry to a majority before commitment; writes still require quorum replication, while the leader provides a single proposed order.

exercises.prompt: Order a Raft-style leader election.
steps: Followers hear nothing from the leader for a timeout
One follower becomes a candidate and increments the term
It requests votes with its last log term and index
A node grants at most one vote in the term, and only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date as its own
With a majority, the candidate becomes leader and starts sending heartbeats
exercises.why: A follower starts an election after missing heartbeats, increments the term, and includes its last log term and index in each vote request. A voter grants at most one vote in that term and rejects a candidate with an older log. That election restriction prevents a candidate missing committed history from winning a majority.

exercises.prompt: What is the 'term' number actually doing?
choices: Counting how long the leader has served
Acting as a logical clock: each election gets a higher term, so any message from an older term is recognisably stale and rejected
exercises.why: A term is a monotonically increasing logical leadership epoch. Nodes reject messages from older terms and update themselves when they observe a newer one, so a delayed former leader cannot continue authoritatively after a later election.

exercises.prompt: Two candidates start elections simultaneously and split the vote — nobody gets a majority. What stops this repeating forever?
choices: Randomized election timeouts — each node waits a different random interval, so one almost always starts first next round and wins uncontested
exercises.why: Identical election timeouts make followers become candidates together and split available votes. Randomized timeouts usually let one follower request votes before the others, increasing the chance that one candidate obtains a majority in that term.

exercises.title: A fencing token lets the resource reject a stale leader
exercises.body: A paused leader can outlive its lease: token 5 pauses, the lease expires, and a new leader receives token 6. The protected resource remembers the highest token accepted. When token 5 resumes, the resource rejects its write because 5 is older than 6.
exercises.note: The resource that receives the side effect must compare tokens. Issuing tokens only at the lock service cannot stop a stale client from writing elsewhere.

exercises.prompt: Storage has accepted fencing token 42. A delayed former leader sends a write with token 41. What must storage do?
choices: Accept it because token 41 was once valid
Reject it because 41 is lower than the highest accepted token 42
Ask the lock service whether process 41 is alive
Accept it if the write arrived within one timeout
exercises.why: Accepting token 42 proves that newer authority exists. The protected resource must reject every lower token, so a paused leader cannot apply a stale write after its lease expires even when that process never learned it was replaced.

exercises.prompt: During an election, what happens to writes?
choices: They stop — there's no leader to sequence them, so the system is unavailable for writes until one is elected
They queue on the old leader
exercises.why: Writes pause from leader loss until a new leader wins an election and can establish log authority. Shorter election timeouts reduce this outage but cause more unnecessary elections during delay spikes; longer timeouts reverse that tradeoff.

exercises.title: Production consensus requires durable protocol state and tested recovery logic
exercises.body: Production Raft and Paxos implementations must preserve agreement across crashes, delayed or reordered messages, elections, and membership changes. They persist terms, votes, and log entries before replying at specific protocol steps. A missed persistence or recovery rule can create two committed histories.
exercises.note: Use a maintained consensus service or library when conflicting decisions would violate correctness. Application code must still handle timeouts and stale leaders safely.

exercises.prompt: Your team proposes implementing Raft in-house for a service that needs leader election. Reaction?
choices: Don't: consensus is notoriously hard to get right, and the failure mode is silent corruption discovered later. Use etcd, ZooKeeper, or your database's built-in election
exercises.why: Consensus safety depends on handling rare combinations of delayed messages, restarts, partial persistence, and concurrent elections. Mature implementations have extensive testing and production fixes for these interleavings, while a subtle local bug can create divergent committed state.

exercises.prompt: Which genuinely need consensus? Select all.
choices: Deciding which database replica is the leader
Distributed locks that must never be held twice
exercises.why: Leadership, lock ownership, and cluster membership require one authoritative value because conflicting answers permit unsafe concurrent actions. Page-view increments can merge after temporary disagreement, so per-increment consensus adds latency without protecting a required invariant.

exercises.prompt: A 3-voter cluster has its leader in Virginia. Follower round-trip times are 12ms to Ohio and 80ms to Frankfurt. Ignoring disk and client time, what is the fastest network wait for the leader to replicate a write to a majority?
exercises.why: A majority of three is two voters, and the leader already supplies one vote, so the fastest quorum needs Ohio's acknowledgement after one 12 ms round trip; it need not wait for Frankfurt. Replica placement therefore sets commit latency. Cross-region voters may still be justified when the required failure domain includes an entire region.

exercises.prompt: Two workers may start the same nightly job. Build the authority path that prevents a paused former holder from applying a stale external effect.
exercises.why: The consensus-backed claim grants one lease with a monotonically increasing token, and the effect target accepts only tokens at least as new as the highest it has seen. If the target ignores fencing, a paused worker can resume after its lease expires and write alongside the new holder even though the lock service elected only one current owner.

exercises.prompt: Build the end-to-end path required by this scenario: Two workers may start the same nightly job. Build the authority path that prevents a paused former holder from applying a stale external effect.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Job Workers → Consensus-backed Claim; Consensus-backed Claim → Fencing Check at Target; Fencing Check at Target → Effect Target. That topology is the evidence for the answer: The consensus-backed claim grants one lease with a monotonically increasing token, and the effect target accepts only tokens at least as new as the highest it has seen. If the target ignores fencing, a paused worker can resume after its lease expires and write alongside the new holder even though the lock service elected only one current owner.

exercises.prompt: You use a lock service, and it says you hold the lock. Is it safe to write?
choices: Yes — that's what the lock means
Not by itself: you might be paused and the lease expired without you noticing, so safety needs a fencing token the storage checks — the lock alone can't stop a client that's stopped listening
Yes, if the lock is fresh
Only if the lock service is CP
exercises.why: A garbage-collection pause can outlast a lock lease, allowing another client to acquire the lock while the paused client still believes it owns it. A monotonically increasing fencing token lets the protected resource reject writes from the expired holder.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of consensus?
choices: It's how distributed systems stay fast

It's the expensive machinery that makes disagreement impossible rather than unlikely — so use it for the few decisions where two answers is a catastrophe, run it inside one region, and don't implement it yourself
It removes the need for replication
exercises.why: Consensus constructs one durable decision through quorum intersection, ordered terms, and log rules despite ambiguous failures. It adds coordination round trips and cannot make progress when a required majority is unreachable.

exercises.prompt: A scheduler lease expires, but the paused old scheduler wakes and sends a job after a new scheduler took over. What protects the worker?
choices: Reject commands carrying an older fencing token
exercises.why: A monotonically increasing fencing token lets the worker recognize newer authority and reject delayed commands from an older lease holder.
